analysis.one_liner: Bars health insurers from denying coverage or setting premiums based on genetic test results.
analysis.headline: The bill drew no cosponsors, never left the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the Public Health Service Act to stop health insurers, in both employer plans and the individual market, from restricting enrollment or adjusting premiums because of predictive genetic information about a person or their family members [S2][S3]. It defines "predictive genetic information" as gene-based data that raises disease risk before any symptoms appear, and it excludes already-manifested conditions and de-identified research data [S3]. It would also protect people who simply request or receive genetic services like testing or counseling [S3]. The bill never moved after being referred to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, people with a genetic predisposition to disease — and their children and other family members — would be protected from being denied health coverage or charged higher premiums because of DNA-based risk information that has not yet produced any symptoms [S2][S3]. It would also make people freer to get genetic tests, since asking for or receiving genetic services could not be used against them [S3].

how_it_helps.text: In the group market (employer plans), the bill would ban adjusting premiums or contributions for a group based on predictive genetic information about any member, dependent, or family member.
In the individual market, the bill would bar insurers from using predictive genetic information as a condition of eligibility or in setting premium rates.

It would also stop plans from restricting enrollment because someone requested or received genetic services, such as testing or counseling, so people would not be penalized for finding out their risk.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers would lose the ability to screen out or surcharge people with unfavorable genetic test results, which could raise premiums for other policyholders in the individual market where risk is otherwise priced person by person [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill covers health insurance only. It does nothing to stop genetic discrimination in life insurance, disability insurance, or long-term care insurance, where the same information could still be used against a person, and it does not address employers' use of genetic information.

By barring insurers from setting premiums based on predictive genetic information, the bill removes a risk-pricing tool; an honest supporter would acknowledge that spreading the cost of people with high genetic risk across all policyholders can raise premiums for everyone in the individual market.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real: without a rule, insurers could decline to cover or charge more to people whose genes predict future illness, which would also make people afraid to take genetic tests their doctors recommend [S3]. The cost is that premiums in the affected markets could rise for everyone, since insurers would no longer be able to price for risk they can detect; the bill also leaves out the related kinds of insurance, life and disability, where genetic discrimination is easiest [S3]. On balance it is a modest, targeted protection that stopped short of a comprehensive one, and it never even reached the stage where those tradeoffs got debated.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee, got no cosponsors, and was never brought up for a vote before the Congress ended [S5][S4].

narrative.text: Representative Cliff Stearns (R-FL) introduced the bill on November 21, 2003.
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, and on December 4, 2003 it was referred to that committee's Subcommittee on Health.
No further action was ever taken; the bill died in subcommittee when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.
Not a single member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers are better off, because they kept the ability to use genetic information in enrollment and pricing decisions; no competing bill advanced in this Congress either.

for.name: Rep. Cliff Stearns
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor; no further floor action followed.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill for the rest of the Congress without a markup or a vote, referring it onward to its Health Subcommittee on December 4, 2003.

against.name: Subcommittee on Health
against.role: Subcommittee of referral, Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after the referral.

sides.party_line_note: With a single Republican sponsor, no cosponsors, and no votes ever taken, the record shows no partisan split at all.

industries.note: The bill would strip insurers of the ability to deny enrollment or raise premiums based on predictive genetic information in both group and individual markets [S2][S3]. Their interest in keeping that underwriting discretion runs against people who carry genetic risk but are not yet sick.

With a rule that seeking a genetic test cannot be used against you in health insurance, more people would have less reason to avoid testing and counseling [S3]. This is a secondary effect, not the bill's stated purpose.
